SI Base Units Metre: The metre (m) has been internationally defined as the length of the path that light travels in a vacuum during a time interval of 1/299 792 458 of a second. It is first introduced as a unit of length in the metric system. And 1 m = 3.2 feet. Second: The second (s) is the time that elapses during 9,192,631,770 cycles of the radiation produced by the transition between two hyperfine levels of the ground state of cesium-133 atom. Kilogram: The kilogram(kg) is the mass equal to the mass of a standard Platinum – Iridium alloy cylinder with 90% platinum and 10% iridium) kept at the International Bureau of Weights and Measures in Paris. It is 4cm high and 4cm in diameter.
Concept to know: Distinction in mN, nm, and Nm: mN refers to milli newton (1 mN = 10-3N), nm represents nano meter (1nm = 10-9m), and Nm represents newton metre which is the unit of work or energy.

1.5 Precision and Significant Figures Activity 1.1 i) Stand in front of a dart board and hit the centre of the board with a dart. ii) Mark the point the dart hits on the board and repeat the process for several times. One of the following may be the observation you made. a) The marked points are neither near the centre nor consistent at anywhere. b) The marked points are close to each other (consistent) but are regardless of proximity to the centre. c) The marked points of the darts are all closely near the vicinity (or proximity) of the centre. d) All the marked points are near the centre and are consistent.

Fig 1.5 (i) Concepts on Accuracy and Precise Measurement What are the conclusions from the different observations made above? Accuracy refers to how close the measurements or observations come to lie at the center of the targeted point. Precision refers to how consistent our results of observations are, regardless of closeness to the centre. Hence accuracy is the measurement of the observations near the targeted (or true) value while precision is getting consistent observations. In other words, if the observations are made near the true value, it gives accuracy. But, the observations consistent to each other irrespective of the true value give precision. The precision and accuracy can better be understood with the support of the following Fig 1.5(ii) Concepts on Accuracy and Precise Measurement Physics, Grade 11 | 8

In the first fig in 1.5, the observation points are near the true value and consistent, hence it is the case of accuracy and precision. In the second fig in 1.5, there is a consistent result of the observation regardless of the true target and it is the case of precision. In the third fig in 1.5, since the measurements are near the true value and inconsistent, it is the case of accuracy but not precision. In the fourth fig in 1.5, neither the data are around the near value nor they are consistent, it is the case of no accuracy and no precision.

A similar activity can be done on a given load. Suppose the loads are said to be 10 kg backpacks. If several measurements are made near 10kg, such as 9.8kg, 10.2 kg, 10.4 kg; the case is of accuracy. But if the measurements made are consistent (or close) regardless of the true value such as 12.5kg, 12.6 kg, and 12.4kg: then it is the case of precision.

A Better Concept to Know: To understand the real-life example of accuracy and precision, measure the wt. of a 10 kg mass in the lab and find 3.4 kg, it is not the accurate value of the measurement. If several other measurements were 3.5 kg, 3.3 kg 3.4 kg and so on, these all represent the precise measurement. You precisely measure the data but not accurately. However, if the measured data are at around 10kg as 10.2 kg, 10.1 kg, 9.9 kg, the data all are precise and accurate too. 1.5.1 Significant Figures:

Significant measure is an art of measuring the physical quantity more accurately and precisely and hence is important in scientific and technical measures. The larger the number of significant figures, the greater is the degree of accuracy. The number of significant digits increases if we measure more precisely with smaller range of uncertainty. The measurement will have some digits that are certain and one digit is uncertain (or guessed). In understanding significant figures in measurements, it is important to realize that the precision of a measured value cannot be more precise than the equipment used for measurement.
